title: Money
intro: Money follows a few simple rules: interest, inflation and fees. Learn those, and banks, car dealers and influencers lose their edge over you. Everything here uses South African figures checked in November 2026.

sections.title: How money moves
points: Interest is the price of borrowing money. When you borrow, you pay it. When you save, you earn it.
Compound interest means you earn interest on your interest. R1,000 a month at 10% a year grows to about R759,000 after 20 years. You only put in R240,000.
Inflation (prices rising over time) quietly eats cash. Money sitting in a 0% account loses buying power every year.
Banks make money on the spread (the gap between what they pay savers and what they charge borrowers), plus fees.
The repo rate is the rate the Reserve Bank (SARB) charges banks. Prime is the base rate banks lend at, normally repo plus 3.5 points.
In September 2026 the SARB raised repo to 7.25%, so prime went to 10.75%. Most home and car loans are priced as prime plus or minus something, so your instalment moves when the SARB moves.

sections.title: Debt: friend or trap
points: Good debt buys something that grows or earns, like a home or a skill. Bad debt buys things that lose value fast, like clothes on store credit.
Your credit score is a number bureaus (companies that keep your borrowing history) give you. It drives the interest rate a bank offers you.
By law you get a free credit report from each credit bureau every year. TransUnion and Experian both offer this online.
If your report has a mistake, you can dispute it with the bureau that issued it, for free.
Paying on time every month matters most. Keep credit card and store card balances low compared to their limits.
The National Credit Act (NCA) is the law that governs lending. Only borrow from lenders registered with the National Credit Regulator (NCR).

sections.title: Growing money
points: Step one is an emergency fund (cash for surprises, like a job loss or a car repair). Aim for 3 to 6 months of expenses in a separate savings account.
A Tax-Free Savings Account (TFSA) lets your money grow with no tax on interest, dividends or growth. From 1 March 2026 the limit is R46,000 a year and R500,000 in your lifetime, per person.
Go over the TFSA limit and SARS charges 40% tax on the excess. Unused yearly space is lost, it does not carry over.
A retirement annuity (RA, a personal retirement fund) is tax-deductible. You can deduct up to 27.5% of your income, capped at R430,000 a year from March 2026.

Under the two-pot system (since September 2024), one-third of new retirement contributions goes to a savings pot. You can withdraw from it once per tax year, minimum R2,000, taxed at your marginal rate (the tax rate on your top slice of income).

Low-cost index funds and ETFs (exchange-traded funds, which buy a whole market in one go) beat most expensive funds over time. Fees matter: R1,000 a month for 30 years grows to about R1.83m at 9% a year, but only R1.35m at 7.5%.

sections.title: Housing: rent vs buy
points: Renting is not 'dead money'. A bond also has dead money: interest, rates, levies, insurance and repairs.
A R1.2m bond over 20 years at prime (10.75%) costs about R12,180 a month. Compare that full cost to your rent, not just the price tag.
Transfer duty (a tax on buying property) is 0% on homes up to R1,210,000 for 2026/27. You still pay bond registration and conveyancing (legal transfer) fees.
A deposit lowers your loan and often gets you a better rate. Banks check your income, expenses, credit record and existing debts.
Bond originators like ooba and BetterBond send one application to several banks so they compete for you. ooba's service is free to you.
First Home Finance (formerly FLISP) is a once-off government subsidy for first-time buyers with household income of R3,501 to R22,000 a month. If you earn above that together, you will not qualify.

sections.title: Cars and car loans
points: A car loses value from day one. Treat it as a cost, not an investment.
Vehicle finance uses the car as security, so it is usually cheaper than an unsecured personal loan.
Small rate gaps add up. A R250,000 car over 72 months costs about R4,730 a month at 10.75%, and about R4,990 at 12.75%. That gap is roughly R19,000 over the loan.

A balloon payment (a big lump sum you owe at the end) lowers the monthly instalment but costs more. With a 30% balloon at 12.75%, the instalment drops to about R4,290, but the total rises to about R384,000.
Total cost of ownership is instalment plus insurance, fuel, services, tyres and tolls. Budget for all of it before you choose a car.
A bigger deposit, a shorter term, no balloon and a clean credit report are what get you a better deal by Q2 2027.

sections.title: Building your own thing
points: Side income is taxable. SARS counts it together with your salary.
For 2026/27, you pay no income tax under 65 if your total taxable income is below R99,000.
If you earn income that is not salary, SARS treats you as a provisional taxpayer. That means you pay tax in advance, by the end of August and the end of February.
Keep records of what you earn and spend on the side hustle. Legitimate business costs can reduce the tax you owe.
You can register a company online with CIPC (the Companies and Intellectual Property Commission). Start as a sole trader first if it is small, and register a company once it grows.
Grow skills and income first. A raise or a client is worth far more than chasing a few extra percent on savings.

do: Pull your free TransUnion and Experian credit reports this month. Dispute any errors.
Open a separate emergency fund account. Automate a debit order on payday.
Write down your full monthly spending for 3 months before the car decision.
Save a car deposit now. Aim to finance with no balloon and a 60-month term or shorter.
Each of you open a TFSA with a low-cost index ETF once the emergency fund is in place.
Check what your employer's retirement fund charges in fees. Avoid two-pot withdrawals unless it is a real emergency.
Run the ooba bond and transfer cost calculator for a home you like, and compare it with your current rent.
ask: What is the interest rate as prime plus or minus, and is it fixed or linked to prime?
What is the total amount I will repay over the full term, including all fees?
Is there a balloon or residual payment in this deal? Show me the quote without one.
What is the monthly service fee and initiation fee, and are they included in the instalment?
What credit life or insurance are you adding, and can I use my own cover instead?
What are the total annual fees on this fund (TER plus platform plus advice fees)?
Are you registered with the FSCA, and what is your FSP number?
watch_out: Forex and crypto 'mentors' selling courses or signals. Most earn from your fees and sign-ups, not from trading.
Guaranteed high returns are a lie. Real investments go up and down.
MLMs (multi-level marketing) where you profit by recruiting people, not by selling to real customers.
Deepfake videos of Ramaphosa, Motsepe or TV presenters promoting investments. The FSCA has warned about these.
Loan sharks (mashonisas) who want to keep your bank card or ID as security. Walk away.
High balloon payments that make a car look affordable. The lump sum does not go away.
Two-pot withdrawals for non-emergencies. You pay tax now and lose years of compound growth.
Paying a website for your credit report. You get one free from each bureau every year.

resources.title: Boss Your Money: Learn the Wealth Creation Formula
resources.source: Nokuhle Kumalo — Pan Macmillan South Africa
resources.why: A South African chartered accountant's practical guide to a first car, contracts, insurance and building wealth on a local salary.
takeaways: Start by tracking monthly income against spending. Extreme frugality is not the route to wealth.
Insure against the things that could bankrupt you, and avoid being overinsured.
It puts price tags on big life events such as having children, so planning is less emotional.
It warns that too many side hustles cause stress, so investing should be central.

resources.title: The Wealth Ladder
resources.access: Buy, about R455 (Exclusive Books). Kindle and Audible too.
resources.why: Shows that the right money move depends on how much you already have: save, invest or grow the business.
takeaways: It splits net worth into levels, and each level needs a different strategy.
Early on, growing your income matters more than investment returns.
Later levels shift towards investing, then towards using wealth well.
It's US-based, so adjust the tax and account details for South Africa.

resources.title: The Art of Spending Money
resources.access: Buy, about R409 (Exclusive Books), about R340 (Readers Warehouse)
resources.why: The other half of money most books skip: spending it well. Useful with a baby and a business budget ahead.
takeaways: It treats spending as a skill, like saving and investing.
It looks at why people spend to impress others, and what brings lasting satisfaction.
It asks what money is for once the basics are covered.

resources.title: Same as Ever
resources.access: Buy, about R309 (Exclusive Books). Kindle too.
resources.why: How to plan around risk and surprises, useful for long-term investing and a business with uneven income.
takeaways: Short chapters on things that never change: behaviour, risk and greed.
Forecasts fail, so preparing for surprises beats predicting them.
Keep a margin of safety in money and in life.

resources.title: Buy Your First Home: South Africa's Ultimate Property Guide for Newbies
resources.source: Zamantungwa Khumalo — Penguin Random House SA
resources.access: Buy (price not checked). E-book on Libby/OverDrive.
resources.why: The clearest South African guide to renting vs buying and the steps of a first purchase.
takeaways: Written for South African first-time buyers.
Walks through bonds, deposits and the buying process.
Check current transfer costs and bond rules, as they change.

resources.title: Things I Wish I Knew: What No One Teaches You About Starting and Growing a Business
resources.source: Andile Khumalo — Penguin Random House SA
resources.access: Buy (price not checked). Exclusive Books, out 3 Aug 2026.
resources.why: A South African founder's honest account of business decisions, useful for running Top Click Media.
takeaways: It draws on real decisions and outcomes rather than formulas.
The author founded I AM AN ENTREPRENEUR, which supports small and medium businesses.
Read a sample before buying.

resources.title: New models for South African consumption, house prices, and mortgage and non-mortgage debt
resources.source: Janine Aron & John Muellbauer — Oxford CSAE Working Paper
resources.why: Research on how SA household debt, interest rates and house prices feed into each other.
takeaways: Non-mortgage debt is a bigger share of SA household debt than in richer countries.
Credit conditions for bonds and for other loans move differently.
House prices and debt can overshoot because buyers assume recent gains will continue.

resources.title: Credit Bureau Monitor, Q2 2025
resources.why: Shows how many South Africans have damaged credit records, and why yours matters for car finance and a bond.
takeaways: Credit bureaus held records for 29.24 million credit-active people in June 2025.
About 10.5 million (roughly 36%) had impaired records.

resources.title: Consumer Credit Market Report, Q1 2026
resources.why: The official quarterly picture of lending in SA: bonds, car finance and unsecured loans.
takeaways: Built from returns that lenders must file under the National Credit Act.
Shows where credit, and risk, is growing.

resources.title: SPIVA South Africa Scorecard, Year-End 2025
resources.why: Tests whether SA fund managers beat a cheap index: the core evidence for index funds and ETFs.
takeaways: 80% of SA equity funds lagged their index in 2025.
66% of global equity funds sold in SA failed to beat the world index.
Over 10 years, about 75% of active funds underperformed on average.

resources.title: Note on the state of household finances in South Africa
resources.source: J Mokoena & K Setshedi — SARB Quarterly Bulletin
resources.why: The Reserve Bank's own look at SA household income, assets and debt: a baseline for your own numbers.
takeaways: Uses household balance-sheet data from 2010 onwards.
Not checked in full yet, so skim it before relying on specific figures.

resources.title: Tax-Free Investments
resources.why: Official TFSA limits (R46,000 a year, R500,000 lifetime) and the 40% penalty.
takeaways: From 1 March 2026 the annual contribution limit is R46,000, replacing R36,000 for earlier tax years.
The lifetime contribution limit remains R500,000 per person across all their tax-free investments.
SARS imposes a 40% tax on contributions above the applicable annual or lifetime limit.
Income, dividends and capital gains inside qualifying accounts are exempt from the relevant South African taxes.
Investment growth does not use contribution room, but withdrawing and reinvesting money counts as a new contribution.
Formal transfers between tax-free accounts have been allowed since 1 March 2018.

resources.title: Rates of Tax for Individuals
resources.why: Current tax tables and the R99,000 tax-free threshold for side-income planning.
takeaways: The 2027 tax year runs from 1 March 2026 to 28 February 2027.
Its first tax band is 18% on taxable income up to R245,100 before rebates.
The top marginal rate is 45% on taxable income above R1,878,600.
A marginal rate [the rate on the next slice of income] does not apply to every rand earned.
The primary rebate for 2026/27 is R17,820.
The under-65 tax threshold is R99,000, with higher thresholds for people aged 65 and older.

resources.title: Free Credit Report
resources.why: Get your free yearly report and dispute errors.
takeaways: Consumers are entitled to a free credit report from each bureau every year.
The lender decides whether to grant credit and at what rate, while the bureau supplies information.
Checking the report can reveal incorrect payment records, personal details or possible identity theft.
Disputes should include supporting records such as payment receipts.
The page's low take-up statistics come from 2014 and should not be treated as today's participation rate.

resources.title: FSP Search
resources.why: Check whether an adviser or investment firm is actually licensed before you pay anything.
takeaways: The FSCA homepage provides an FSP [financial services provider] search entry point.
It also directs users to lists of regulated insurers, investment schemes and retirement funds.
The warnings section identifies suspected unauthorised firms and impersonation schemes.
Its regulatory publications and actions provide context beyond the mere existence of a licence.
Use the actual search service to confirm authorisation rather than treating the homepage itself as a completed check.

resources.title: FSCA warning: These well-known people cannot help you to invest
resources.why: How deepfake investment scams work in SA.
takeaways: The June 2025 report describes fake investment promotions using Patrice Motsepe, Leanne Manas, Cyril Ramaphosa and Paul Mashatile.
One scheme promised R13,000 to R17,000 a day from only R4,500 invested.
Fraudsters also impersonated Momentum executives and legitimate brokers through WhatsApp and Telegram groups.
The FSCA warned that scammers use its logo, staff details and fake certificates.
A copied FSP number is insufficient because the name and permitted category of service must also match.
The report recommends independently confirming authorisation with the FSCA before paying money.

resources.title: Two-pot withdrawals: What you need to know
resources.why: Plain explainer of the savings pot, the R2,000 minimum and the tax hit.
takeaways: The article dates the two-pot launch to 1 September 2024.
Generally one-third of new contributions enters the savings pot and two-thirds enters the retirement pot.
Pre-launch money normally sits in a vested component under earlier rules.
The savings pot generally permits one withdrawal per tax year with a R2,000 minimum.
Withdrawals are taxed as ordinary income and may attract fund administration charges.
Resignation does not unlock the retirement component, while leaving savings invested preserves potential compound growth.

resources.title: Just One Lap
resources.why: Independent SA site on ETFs and tax-free investing, with a JSE ETF database.
takeaways: The site separates money skills, investing education and trading material.
Its Investing 101 and ETF reviews provide South African starting points for understanding funds.
Tax Tuesday and tax-free investing sections connect investing with local tax questions.
An ETF database and dividend calendar support research beyond introductory articles.
Power Hour videos and podcasts add spoken explanations, while the site identifies sponsors separately.

resources.title: 10X Investments
resources.why: Low-fee index retirement annuities and TFSAs. Shows why fees matter.
takeaways: 10X offers retirement annuities, preservation funds, living annuities, unit trusts and tax-free investments.
Its published approach emphasises asset allocation [the mix of investments], diversification and managing fees.
The site provides EAC, retirement, tax-free and two-pot calculators.
Its MSCI World feeder option is offered through certain products, which does not mean every retirement product can invest entirely offshore.
The homepage promotes direct investing without adviser or broker fees and provides a route to calculate product-specific costs.
These are the provider's product descriptions and marketing claims rather than an independent comparison of all available providers.

resources.title: EasyEquities
resources.why: Low-cost platform to buy ETFs in a TFSA with no minimums.
takeaways: EasyEquities offers company shares, ETFs and separate tax-free and retirement account options.
Its whole-share disclosure says investors receive ownership and the associated economic rights.
An FSR [fractional security right] is instead a contractual derivative claim against EasyEquities until a whole share is delivered.
FSRs do not carry the voting rights of whole shares.
The platform distinguishes self-selected investments from managed bundles that involve a manager's fee.
Its costs and Thrive pages must be read alongside fund charges because easy account access does not establish the total investment cost.

resources.title: Bond and Transfer Costs Calculator
resources.why: See the real upfront cost of buying, beyond the deposit.
takeaways: The supplied older link was unavailable during checking, but ooba's current Transfer Cost Calculator was found and checked.
The calculator estimates bond-registration and property-transfer costs rather than only monthly repayments.
The loan amount and property purchase details affect the estimated costs.
Bond registration and ownership transfer are different legal steps with different charges.
Use the estimate for budgeting and obtain the actual conveyancer and lender quotations before committing.

resources.title: First Home Finance
resources.why: Official criteria for the first-time buyer subsidy (formerly FLISP).
takeaways: NHFC's current First Home Finance page describes a once-off subsidy to help qualifying households buy or build a first home.
The listed gross household income range is R3,501 to R22,000 a month.
Applicants must be adult South African citizens or legal permanent residents who can enter a contract.
Applicants must not previously have owned a home or benefited from a government housing programme.
The listed criteria include finance approval or in-principle approval through an eligible lender or approved partner.
The programme allows several approved funding routes, including pension-backed lending, savings and certain community or employer schemes.

resources.title: Balloon payment warning for car buyers in South Africa
resources.why: Why balloon deals keep people paying for cars longer.
takeaways: The June 2024 article reports that a third of Standard Bank's relevant customers had chosen the maximum balloon over the preceding year.
The bank reported a 41% rise over five years in new-vehicle purchases using balloon payments.
A balloon moves part of the debt to the end of the contract rather than removing it.
The lower monthly payment can leave the borrower needing to refinance the final amount.
The reported adoption figures belong to that bank and period rather than every South African car buyer.

resources.title: CIPC
resources.why: Where you register a company when the side hustle grows.
takeaways: CIPC [Companies and Intellectual Property Commission] handles company registration and continuing company compliance.
A company's annual return to CIPC is separate from its tax return to SARS.
Companies must file annual returns even when they have not traded.
CIPC requires current beneficial-ownership information [who ultimately owns or controls the entity] with annual-return compliance.
From 1 July 2024 its filing system prevents annual-return submission unless beneficial-ownership information is current.
Persistent non-compliance can lead to deregistration rather than simply an unpaid administration fee.

resources.title: The Psychology of Money
resources.why: Best book on money behaviour. Short chapters, no jargon.
takeaways: The publisher presents money behaviour as a major driver of outcomes alongside financial knowledge.
Housel uses 19 short stories rather than presenting a mathematical investing formula.
The description highlights personal history, ego, pride, marketing and incentives as influences on real decisions.
Financial decisions happen in families and workplaces rather than only inside spreadsheets.
The listed 2020 book is a behavioural introduction rather than a source of current South African tax or product rules.

resources.title: How to Make Your First Million
resources.why: SA financial planner on how ordinary South Africans built wealth.
takeaways: The publisher describes the goal as building a first R1 million in savings and investments.
The book uses examples of ordinary people who reached financial goals through different routes.
Its definition of financial freedom centres on living from the income of savings and investments.
The linked edition is Warren Ingram's 176-page book published in August 2016.
These points are verified from the publisher's description rather than a full-text reading, and the edition predates two-pot retirement rules.

resources.title: Honest Money (podcast)
resources.why: 350+ SA episodes on investing, retirement and money habits. No hype.
takeaways: The podcast is hosted by financial planner and author Warren Ingram, with Pieter de Villiers appearing in the current episode catalogue.
The October 2026 catalogue includes an episode comparing debt repayment with investing.
Another October 2026 episode examines lump-sum versus monthly investing and the psychology of timing.
A five-year R200,000 goal episode discusses medium-term investing and risk management.
The catalogue also addresses starting on a small salary, platform fees, insurance and estate planning.
These are verified episode-description takeaways from the current catalogue rather than a claim that every episode has been listened to.

resources.title: Monetary policy: who sets interest rates and why
resources.why: Read the institution's explanation of rates, inflation and the delay before policy affects households.
takeaways: South Africa's inflation target is 3% with a tolerance band of one percentage point on either side.
The Minister of Finance determines the target in agreement with the SARB Governor.
The Monetary Policy Committee meets six times a year to decide the repo rate.
SARB estimates that policy changes work through the economy over roughly 12 to 24 months.
Temporary inflation deviations are allowed because trying to offset every price shock could destabilise economic activity.

resources.title: SARB position on the necessity of a retail CBDC: Background Note
resources.why: Start with pages 6 to 9 for a grounded account of bank money before exploring digital-currency claims.
takeaways: The 57-page note distinguishes central bank cash from commercial bank demand deposits.
Commercial bank deposits are liabilities of the bank and are created mainly through credit extension.
A loan appears as a bank asset and the matching deposit as a bank liability.
Deposits can also arise when cash is deposited or a bank buys a financial asset.
A CBDC [central bank digital currency] would differ from an ordinary banking-app balance because it would be central bank money.
The note examines cash access and payment inclusion as well as technical experiments, rather than presenting new technology alone as a reason to issue a CBDC.

resources.title: CODI frequently asked questions
resources.why: Bookmark this to distinguish protected bank savings from investments sold by a bank.
takeaways: Cover is capped at R100,000 per qualifying depositor per bank, including interest.
Protection is automatic and depositors do not pay CODI directly.
Qualifying products include transactional, savings, notice and fixed-term deposit accounts.
Shares, ETFs, unit trusts and retirement annuities are investment products outside this deposit cover.
The FAQ's joint-account example splits R180,000 equally, then combines each person's share with their other qualifying balances at that bank.
Amounts above the limit remain claims against the failed bank's estate rather than receiving guaranteed full repayment.

resources.title: Battle of the banks 2025: Capitec vs Standard Bank vs FNB vs Absa vs Nedbank
resources.why: A concrete comparison of bank scale and earnings with useful warnings about comparing unlike figures.
takeaways: The article compares the big five banks across 13 measures rather than declaring one bank biggest in every sense.
Capitec leads on customer numbers, while Standard Bank leads on assets.
FirstRand's quoted market value is about R448.9 billion in this September 2025 snapshot.
The cited PwC analysis puts combined first-half 2025 headline earnings at R69.7 billion, up 11.2% year on year.
The comparison combines June 2025, February 2025 and December 2024 year ends.
Group finances and South African customer figures have different scopes, so group profit is not profit earned only from local retail customers.

resources.title: National Credit Regulator: registers, complaints and credit data
resources.why: The main starting point for checking a lender or counsellor and challenging credit-industry conduct.
takeaways: The NCR was established under the National Credit Act 34 of 2005.
It registers credit providers, credit bureaus, debt counsellors and payment distribution agents.
Its remit includes consumer education, complaint investigations and enforcement of the Act.
The site publishes a Consumer Credit Market Report and a Credit Bureau Monitor.
The site provides registrant lists and a complaints route rather than lending money itself.

resources.title: Debt counselling: a debt relief measure for over-indebted consumers
resources.why: Understand the consequences before agreeing to a debt-review sales call.
takeaways: Debt counselling helps people whose income cannot cover living expenses and debt repayments.
It restructures payments rather than cancelling debt or creating a savings plan.
A lower payment can extend the repayment period.
The NCR registers the individual debt counsellor, whose name and registration number must be supplied.
A debt-counselling indicator appears on the credit profile and access to further credit is restricted.
The service has fees, which the NCR says should be disclosed in writing before application.

resources.title: Guidelines for complaints relating to disputed consumer credit information
resources.why: A practical escalation map when a bureau keeps an incorrect debt or payment record.
takeaways: Dispute the information with the relevant credit bureau before asking the NCR to investigate.
The bureau must supply a dispute reference number.
Allow the bureau 20 business days to investigate the complaint.
If dissatisfied, submit the NCR complaint using Form 29 with dates, supporting records and the bureau reference.
The guideline specifies a 20-business-day escalation window after receiving the bureau's supporting evidence or findings.
Skipping the initial bureau complaint can prevent the NCR from taking jurisdiction under this process.

resources.title: ASISA member standards: costs and investment reporting
resources.source: Association for Savings and Investment South Africa
resources.why: Bookmark the original disclosure standards to ask providers precise questions about fees.
takeaways: The library separates total expense ratio and transaction-cost standards from the retail EAC standard.
EAC [effective annual cost] estimates the annualised impact of charges over specified periods.
The linked retail standard groups costs into investment management, advice, administration and other charges.
Different holding periods can produce different EAC figures because early and continuing charges have different effects.
Separate standards address retirement savings cost disclosure and EAC for individual retirement fund members.
ASISA represents industry members, so its standards are disclosure tools rather than independent product recommendations.

resources.title: Costs, fees and commissions: how do these impact your investment?
resources.source: Moneyweb Financial Advisor Views, Dawn Ridler of Rexsolom Invest
resources.why: A detailed fee-layer explainer whose adviser-authored perspective should be kept visible.
takeaways: An additional annual fee of 1% to 2% costs R10,000 to R20,000 on R1 million before lost future growth.
A fund of funds [a fund holding other funds] can add another layer of charges.
The article describes upfront investment commissions of around 3% as an older charging approach.
Continuing adviser charges can be based on assets, while other models include a retainer, a plan fee or hourly billing.
It recommends comparing the combined EAC rather than one advertised fee.
The author is an adviser defending the value of advice, so her examples are not a universal tariff or proof that any quoted fee is justified.

resources.title: Unscrupulous lenders continue to fleece vulnerable debtors
resources.source: Stellenbosch University, reporting on Stephan van der Merwe's Law Clinic investigation
resources.why: A documented investigation of payroll deductions that shows the limits of assuming formal systems protect everyone.
takeaways: The investigation examined credit agreements, affordability schedules, payslips, creditor statements and debtor accounts.
It found payroll deductions reaching about 75% of wages in some investigated cases.
One example involved a R11,178 loan deduction against a monthly salary of R15,041.
The report describes lenders rolling outstanding balances into new loans.
In one calculation, credit insurance cost about R32,000 on a R97,000 loan, compared with about R19,000 if based on the declining balance.
These are documented cases from an investigation, not a representative estimate for all South African borrowers.

resources.title: Home sweet home: Should you rent or buy?
resources.why: Challenges the idea that renting is automatically wasted money using South African ownership costs.
takeaways: The article recommends considering buying when expecting to stay in the same home for eight years or longer.
It counts rates, levies, maintenance, legal costs, interest and insurance alongside the purchase price.
A disciplined renter can invest the difference between rent and the full ownership cost.
For sectional-title homes, it recommends investigating the body corporate's finances and unpaid levies.
It recommends an emergency fund covering at least six months of total monthly homeownership costs.
The eight-year suggestion is the author's rule of thumb, while local prices, rents and financing determine an actual break-even point.

resources.title: City of Ekurhuleni municipal tariffs
resources.why: Use the local authority's schedules to test the real monthly cost of an Edenvale home.
takeaways: The page provides the 2026/27 municipal tariff schedules rather than one all-inclusive household rate.
Schedule 1 covers assessment rates [property taxes].
Schedule 2 covers electricity and identifies an updated schedule aligned with NERSA-approved rates.
Schedules 3, 4 and 5 cover water, sewerage and waste management separately.
The library also includes building-control and city-planning charges that can matter when altering a property.
The applicable account category and usage determine the bill, so a neighbouring household's total is not a substitute for the schedules.

resources.title: How vehicle finance with a balloon payment works
resources.why: A lender's own worked example makes the postponed debt visible, with a clear commercial interest to keep in mind.
takeaways: Its R400,000 car example uses a 20% balloon, leaving R80,000 payable at the end.
The monthly capital repayments reduce the other R320,000 rather than eliminating the final R80,000.
Interest is still charged on the unpaid balloon balance during the agreement.
A balloon delays the point at which the car's trade-in value catches up with the outstanding debt.
The article suggests planning for the final amount through extra repayment or dedicated saving.
It also raises insurance shortfall cover, whose terms need checking because ordinary vehicle value can be less than the loan balance.

resources.title: Budget 2026 frequently asked questions
resources.why: Check current thresholds here before following an older South African money guide.
takeaways: The 2026/27 retirement contribution deduction cap rises to R430,000, alongside the 27.5% limit.
Unused retirement contributions can carry forward rather than automatically disappearing.
The under-65 annual South African interest exemption remains R23,800.
SARS says it administers a R2.3 million compulsory VAT-registration threshold and R120,000 voluntary threshold from 1 April 2026 while noting that the amendments await promulgation.
The FAQ excludes some professional-service and personal-service businesses from turnover tax, so small turnover alone does not establish eligibility.
A registered VAT vendor must keep accounting for VAT until its registration is formally cancelled.

resources.title: Tax implications of withdrawing from the Two-Pot Retirement System
resources.why: The tax authority explains why the amount requested is different from the cash received.
takeaways: Applicants must be registered for tax before the fund requests a withdrawal directive.
SARS can reject a directive request if the member is not tax registered.
The withdrawal is taxed using the individual's applicable income-tax rate.
The release warns that outstanding SARS debt can be deducted from the payout.
Any over-deduction or under-deduction of tax is settled through the annual assessment.
The release points members to digital channels and a calculator rather than requiring a SARS branch visit.

resources.title: Two-pot retirement reform in a nutshell
resources.why: A launch-era explainer that connects withdrawal mechanics with tax and fund administration.
takeaways: People with earlier retirement savings generally have vested, savings and retirement components.
The launch transferred 10% of eligible vested savings to the savings component, capped at R30,000 per fund.
Its R200,000 vested-balance example produces R20,000 of seed capital.
A withdrawal request goes through the fund administrator rather than paying out automatically.
The article reported expected administration fees of R300 to R600 at launch, which are historical examples rather than current universal prices.
It warns that a request cannot simply be cancelled once the administrator has obtained the relevant tax directive, so calculate the net proceeds first.

resources.title: Provisional tax
resources.why: Essential for a salaried person who begins earning freelance or business income.
takeaways: Provisional tax is a way to pay income tax in advance, not an additional tax on top of income tax.
It generally requires two estimated payments during the tax year and allows an optional third payment afterwards.
Payments are credited against the final assessed income-tax liability.
Business income can bring an individual into the system, while statutory exclusions apply to some non-business income.
Companies automatically fall within the provisional-tax system.
Taxpayers must determine their own status and request the IRP6 [provisional tax return] through eFiling.

resources.title: Sole proprietorship
resources.why: Explains the simplest business structure and the personal risks hidden behind its simplicity.
takeaways: A sole proprietorship belongs to one individual and has no separate legal existence.
The owner includes business income in their own income-tax return.
Using a trading name does not create a separate legal entity.
The owner is personally liable for business debts, potentially exposing personal property.
Simple establishment and direct control come with limits on capital and the skills available from one owner.

resources.title: Legal but reckless: Lending to social grant recipients
resources.source: GroundUp opinion, Erin Torkelson, Deborah James and David Neves
resources.why: Research-based historical analysis of how formal financial inclusion can become a debt-extraction system.
takeaways: The authors draw on Black Sash and London School of Economics research rather than discussing only informal loan sharks.
The 2012 grant-payment contract opened about 10 million bank accounts and created a large market for financial products.
Automatic collection could give lenders access to grant money before recipients could spend it.
The article's historical R1,000 loan illustration reaches R1,750 over six months after interest and fees.
The authors argue that small debts can be devastating as a share of household income even when small in national lending statistics.
Its interest and fee figures describe the 2020 analysis and should not be used as a current legal price schedule.

resources.title: FAIS Ombud: how to complain
resources.source: Office of the Ombud for Financial Services Providers
resources.why: A practical complaint route when advice or intermediary services may have caused financial harm.
takeaways: The office provides a complaints registration form and an online submission option.
The page asks complainants to check the pre-requisites before submitting.
Supporting records should include correspondence, policy or application documents and the contact details of the person involved.
Paper complaint forms must be signed to be accepted.
The office offers assistance with completing the form and a complaint-status route.

resources.title: Manage Your Money Like a F*cking Grownup
resources.why: A direct South African introduction that connects money habits, earning power and family obligations.
takeaways: The publisher describes practical work on budgeting and understanding credit rather than a stock-tip manual.
It covers negotiating a raise as well as controlling spending.
It challenges the assumption that buying a house will automatically make the owner rich.
It addresses black tax [financial support for extended family] as a real planning issue.
The listed 248-page edition uses exercises, flowcharts and illustrations.
These points come from the publisher's description of the 2018 edition, whose tax figures need checking against current SARS guidance.

resources.title: Standard Bank Power Hour: Getting Started in Shares
resources.source: Simon Brown / Just One Lap, hosted by Standard Bank
resources.why: A locally taught recorded introduction with the host bank's sponsorship clearly visible.
takeaways: The host page dates the recording to 18 April 2024.
Its stated syllabus covers company shares, dividends [payments to shareholders], tax and ETFs.
The broader Power Hour listing describes portfolio design and offshore exposure as part of this session.
Standard Bank hosts the event, so the presentation has a commercial sponsor.
These are verified syllabus points from the host pages rather than claims based on a viewed transcript, and 2024 tax figures require updating.

resources.title: The Fat Wallet: Figuring out investment fees
resources.source: Kristia van Heerden and Simon Brown / Just One Lap
resources.why: A specific listener case shows how difficult it can be to discover the price of a longstanding investment.
takeaways: The show notes describe a listener who invested for 16 years before investigating her charges.
The hosts say it took about two weeks to work through the statements and reach an answer.
The case included nearly 30 funds in one account plus a second investment account.
The notes distinguish fund management, platform administration and initial or continuing adviser charges.
A percentage fee can rise in rands as the portfolio grows even when contributions do not increase.
The quoted provider prices belong to a 2018 case and should be used to learn the audit method rather than to rank providers today.

who_pays: Households pay banks through loan interest, account charges and payment fees.
Investors pay fund managers, platforms and advisers through charges that often come straight out of their investments.
Workers and employers fund retirement contributions, while workers bear the cost of early withdrawals and weak investment returns.
Taxpayers fund housing subsidies and public services through taxes collected by SARS [South African Revenue Service].
Member banks fund CODI [Corporation for Deposit Insurance], which protects qualifying deposits within its coverage limit.
who_decides: Parliament makes tax and credit laws, while SARS administers taxes and Treasury develops financial policy.
SARB [South African Reserve Bank] sets monetary policy through its Monetary Policy Committee, while banks set individual lending offers.
The Prudential Authority supervises financial institutions' safety, while the FSCA [Financial Sector Conduct Authority] regulates market conduct.
The NCR [National Credit Regulator] enforces the NCA [National Credit Act] and registers lenders, credit bureaus and debt counsellors.
Lenders decide credit applications using their own rules and bureau information, while retirement fund rules determine members' investment and withdrawal options.
who_profits: Banks earn net interest income [interest received minus interest paid] and income from fees and other services.
Shareholders receive dividends and changes in share value, including pension funds that own bank shares.
Fund managers and platforms can collect charges even when an investor loses money.
Advisers may earn product commissions, initial fees or continuing charges based on the assets they advise on.
Credit bureaus sell information services, while property transactions generate business for estate agents, conveyancers and home-loan providers.
what_it_means_for_us: Build the household plan around essential expenses, available cash and goals before choosing products.
Compare the total rand cost and exit conditions of each offer, including every investment fee and any final loan balloon.
Keep separate records of Sean's and Mishka's tax-free contributions because the limits belong to individuals.
Use regulators' registers and complaint routes to challenge bad information or treatment without assuming a licence guarantees a good product.
Treat the dated rules here as checked on 15 November 2026 and revisit official sources before a tax filing, withdrawal or major purchase.

deep_sections.title: Money is a promise, and banks have constraints
points: A bank deposit is the bank's debt to you, while physical cash is central bank money.
SARB's 2025 money background note explains how bank lending creates matching loans and deposits.
A bank records a loan as an asset [money owed to it] and a deposit as a liability [money it owes].
Creating deposits does not give banks unlimited spending power because lending brings funding needs, credit losses and regulatory constraints.
Bank profits must be assessed after funding costs, operating costs and bad debts rather than treating all interest receipts as profit.
BusinessTech's bank comparison mixes different financial year ends, so its figures cannot be read as one identical reporting period.
The repo rate [SARB's policy interest rate] influences borrowing costs but does not determine the exact rate on your loan.
SARB now targets 3% inflation with a tolerance band of one percentage point on either side.
SARB says policy changes typically affect the economy over roughly 12 to 24 months.
Lower inflation means prices rise more slowly rather than returning to their old level.
CODI covers up to R100,000 per qualifying depositor per bank across qualifying deposits, including interest.
Several accounts at the same bank share that deposit-insurance limit.
A bank money-market deposit can qualify for cover, while a money-market unit trust is an investment outside CODI's cover.
A return is real [adjusted for inflation] only after accounting for the loss of buying power.

deep_sections.title: Credit is a contract, not a character score
points: A bureau supplies credit information, while the lender makes the approval decision.
A high credit score cannot make a loan affordable if repayments leave too little for living costs.
TransUnion's page explains that errors and identity theft can affect the report used by a lender.
The NCR's dispute guidance requires a bureau investigation before escalation to the regulator.
Keep the dispute reference and payment evidence so the complaint can be traced.
A quoted monthly instalment hides the loan term, interest, service fees, insurance and any final balance.
A balloon [a lump sum postponed until the end] reduces monthly capital repayment without forgiving the postponed debt.
Interest continues on the outstanding balloon balance during the loan.
Negative equity [owing more than the car can sell for] makes changing cars expensive.
A deposit and a shorter repayment term reduce debt exposure but must leave enough cash for emergencies.
Debt consolidation replaces debts with a new loan, while debt counselling restructures repayments through the NCA process.
Debt counselling does not cancel debt and usually prevents further borrowing while the process applies.
A debt counsellor's own NCR registration must be checked even when the service uses a familiar company name.
GroundUp's historical grant-lending analysis shows how a legally permitted price can still be harmful for a vulnerable household.
Stellenbosch Law Clinic's payroll investigation shows why deductions deserve scrutiny even when an employer processes them.

deep_sections.title: The investment and its tax wrapper are different choices
points: A TFSA [tax-free savings account] is a tax treatment, while an ETF [exchange-traded fund] is an investment that may fit inside it.
For the 2027 tax year from 1 March 2026 to 28 February 2027, SARS lists the annual TFSA contribution limit as R46,000 per person.
The TFSA lifetime contribution limit remains R500,000 per person across providers.
Investment growth inside a TFSA does not use contribution room.
Withdrawing TFSA money does not restore contribution room when that money is paid back.
Use a formal provider transfer to move a TFSA instead of withdrawing and depositing the cash yourself.
An RA [retirement annuity] offers contribution tax deductions in exchange for retirement access restrictions.
SARS lists a 2026/27 deduction ceiling of 27.5% of the greater of remuneration or taxable income, subject to the R430,000 annual cap and statutory calculation rules.
That deduction limit covers pension, provident and RA contributions together.
A tax deduction reduces taxable income rather than refunding the entire amount invested.
Retirement withdrawals and retirement income can be taxed later, so an RA is not a promise that all future benefits are tax-free.
Regulation 28 [retirement fund investment rules] limits portfolio exposures, so an RA has different investment constraints from a discretionary account.
Under two-pot rules, generally one-third of new contributions goes to the savings component and two-thirds to the retirement component.
Older savings normally remain in a vested component [money governed by earlier access rules], so many people actually have three components.
The savings component permits a minimum R2,000 withdrawal generally once per tax year per fund, subject to eligibility and fund rules.
A two-pot withdrawal adds taxable income and can lose both administration charges and future compound growth.
Available cash, expected tax relief and time until the goal should determine the choice between ordinary savings, a TFSA and retirement saving.

deep_sections.title: Compounding rewards patience and also compounds fees
points: An index [a rule-based market measure] is a benchmark rather than something you can buy directly.
An index fund aims to track an index through an investable portfolio.
An ETF can hold shares, bonds or other exposures, so the ETF label alone does not tell you its risk.
A global equity fund bought in rands still carries foreign-market and currency exposure.
Several funds can hold the same large companies, so counting fund names does not measure diversification [spreading exposure].
SPIVA's year-end 2025 study found 94% of South African equity funds lagged its capped composite benchmark over ten years.
The same study found only 32% of short-term bond funds lagged their benchmark over ten years, so active management results differ by category.
Survivorship bias [ignoring funds that closed or merged] can make investment results look better than investors actually experienced.
A benchmark return is not the return of a purchasable ETF after its fees and trading costs.
The TER [total expense ratio] does not capture every cost an investor pays.
EAC [effective annual cost] estimates the combined effect of investment, advice, administration and other charges over stated periods.
Ask for EAC figures for the same contribution amount and holding period before comparing products.
Illustrative arithmetic: R100,000 growing at 8% a year for 30 years becomes about R1,006,266 before tax.
Illustrative arithmetic: reducing that annual growth to 6% leaves about R574,349 after 30 years.
Those calculations assume constant annual returns and no further contributions rather than predicting market performance.
Ask an adviser for the rand cost, payment model, conflicts and work delivered before accepting a recurring percentage fee.
An FSCA licence must match the firm, person and service being offered because scammers can copy genuine licence numbers.

deep_sections.title: Housing and business decisions are cash-flow decisions
points: Rent buys housing services, while buying adds a concentrated property investment financed by a long debt contract.
Compare rent with interest, rates, levies, insurance, maintenance and transaction costs rather than with the bond instalment alone.
Capital repayment [reducing the loan balance] builds equity rather than disappearing as an expense.
Buying also ties up a deposit that could otherwise earn an investment return.
Daily Maverick's suggested eight-year holding period is a planning rule of thumb rather than a universal break-even date.
Compare actual Edenvale sale prices and rents for similar homes because Cape Town price growth is not a Johannesburg forecast.
Check sectional-title body corporate accounts and maintenance plans for possible special levies [extra charges to owners].
Ekurhuleni publishes separate rates, electricity, water, sewerage and waste schedules for the 2026/27 municipal year.
Illustrative arithmetic: a R1 million loan over 20 years at a constant 10% costs about R9,650 a month before fees and insurance.
Illustrative arithmetic: the same loan at a constant 12% costs about R11,011 a month before fees and insurance.
The 10% example repays about R1.316 million in interest over 20 years if payments and the rate never change.
A longer loan can lower the instalment while increasing total interest.
A side business should track sales, costs and unpaid invoices separately from household spending.
A sole proprietor [an individual trading in their own capacity] declares business income on their personal tax return and carries personal liability.
Private spending does not become a business deduction simply because it is paid from a business account.
SARS generally requires deductible business expenditure to be incurred for trade and producing income, with separate rules for capital assets.
Provisional tax [advance income-tax payments] can apply to side-business income even when PAYE [tax withheld from salary] already covers a day job.
A company adds CIPC annual-return and beneficial-ownership duties alongside its SARS obligations.
The SARS Budget 2026 FAQ says it administers the R2.3 million compulsory VAT threshold from 1 April 2026 while noting the legislative process.
Use the VAT threshold for taxable supplies [sales counted under VAT rules] rather than treating it as a profit threshold.
Set aside tax from business receipts before treating the remaining cash as available household income.
